label: Other Representations of Rotations
notes: This appendix spans printed pages 575 to 584 and asks why so many rotation coordinates exist. Each chart describes the same element of SO(3) but trades minimality, freedom from singularities, and composition cost differently. We keep the invariant rotation fixed and watch how the coordinates behave throughout the lecture.

label: The Object: SO(3)
notes: Every representation in this appendix encodes one object: a rotation in SO(3), a real three by three matrix with orthonormal columns and determinant one. The group is a curved three dimensional manifold, so no single set of three numbers can chart it smoothly everywhere without a singularity.

label: Euler Angles (ZYX)
notes: Euler angles factor a rotation into three elementary turns about coordinate axes. The ZYX convention rotates by yaw about z, then pitch about y, then roll about x. Three numbers give a minimal, human readable chart, but the meaning depends entirely on the chosen axis order and frame.

label: Roll-Pitch-Yaw
notes: Roll-pitch-yaw is the space fixed cousin of Euler angles, composing rotations about the fixed world axes rather than the moving body axes. It is intuitive for vehicles and aircraft, yet it inherits the same three parameter structure and therefore the same unavoidable coordinate singularity at certain pitch values.

label: Gimbal Lock
notes: When the middle rotation aligns two of the gimbal axes, the first and third rotations turn about the same line and one degree of freedom collapses in the coordinates. This gimbal lock is a chart failure, not a physical one: the rigid body can still rotate freely in every direction.

label: Exponential Coordinates
notes: Exponential coordinates pack the rotation axis and angle into a single three vector omega-hat times theta. The matrix exponential recovers the rotation through Rodrigues' formula. This chart is minimal and geometrically natural, singular only at angle multiples of two pi where the direction of the axis becomes undefined.

label: Unit Quaternions
notes: A unit quaternion stores a rotation as four numbers constrained to the unit sphere in four dimensions. The scalar part is cosine of half the angle and the vector part is the axis scaled by sine of half the angle, giving a smooth global container with no gimbal lock.

label: The Double Cover S^3 to SO(3)
notes: The unit three sphere double covers SO(3): the quaternions q and minus q name the exact same rotation. This two to one map explains why four constrained numbers represent a three dimensional group, and why naive interpolation must watch for sign flips along a trajectory.

label: Quaternion Composition and Conversion
notes: Quaternion multiplication composes rotations directly, costing far fewer operations than multiplying matrices and staying numerically stable under repeated products. A fixed bilinear formula converts any unit quaternion into its rotation matrix, so attitude can move freely between the two representations whenever a computation demands it.

label: Cayley-Rodrigues Parameters
notes: The Cayley-Rodrigues parameters scale the rotation axis by the tangent of half the angle, building the rotation from a rational Cayley transform without trigonometric functions. The chart is compact and algebraically clean, but its norm blows up at a rotation by pi, which the chart excludes entirely.

label: Comparing the Representations
notes: We close by comparing the charts on parameter count, singularities, and composition cost. Three angle conventions are minimal but lock; exponential coordinates are minimal and natural; quaternions are smooth and cheap to compose; Cayley parameters are rational yet exclude pi. The invariant is always the rotation, never the chart.
